source.spoken_script: A dying man's last words. And they were a child's prayer. Jewish tradition made these words an evening prayer. Words a child could learn for the dark. Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth. On the cross, the three hours of darkness have passed. With his last breath, he prays those evening words. Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. He begins with a word the Psalm does not have. Father. Not judge. Not stranger. Father. The Psalm he prayed says, thou hast redeemed me. On that cross, he was buying that redemption. He dies like a child falling asleep in his father's arms. On the third day, morning came. Because he rose, death loses its last word over everyone who is his. You can close your eyes in those same hands. Not because death is small. Because the hands are strong. platforms.description:
A dying man's last words (Luke 23:46). And they were a child's prayer.

Jewish tradition made Psalm 31:5 an evening prayer, words a child could learn for the dark: into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth.

On the cross, after the three hours of darkness, Jesus prays those evening words with his last breath: "And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost" (Luke 23:46, KJV).

And he begins with a word the Psalm does not have. Father. Not judge. Not stranger. Father.

The Psalm he prayed says thou hast redeemed me. On that cross, he was buying that redemption. He dies like a child falling asleep in his father's arms. And on the third day, morning came.

You can close your eyes in those same hands. Not because death is small. Because the hands are strong. He keeps the morning.

platforms.title: Into Thy Hands: The Bedtime Psalm Jesus Died Praying
platforms.description:
The last words of Jesus on the cross (Luke 23:46) were not composed in the moment. They were a quotation, and by long Jewish tradition, an evening prayer: words a child could learn to say against the dark.

Psalm 31:5: "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O LORD God of truth."

After the three hours of darkness had passed, Jesus prayed those evening words with his final breath: "And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost" (Luke 23:46, KJV).

But listen to the first word. Father. The Psalm does not have it. The dying Son adds it. Not judge. Not stranger. Father.

And the line he prayed says thou hast redeemed me - while on that very cross he was buying that redemption. He dies the way the prayer was meant to be prayed: like a child falling asleep in his father's arms. On the third day, morning came.

In this piece: the evening-prayer tradition behind Psalm 31:5, the one added word, the redemption clause inside the prayer, and why the resurrection turns a deathbed into a bedtime.

You can close your eyes in those same hands. Not because death is small. Because the hands are strong. Commend your spirit to the Father, tonight and every night. He keeps the morning.
